Measures of centre

Mean

xˉ=1n∑i=1nxi\bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_ixˉ=n1​i=1∑n​xi​xˉ=∑fixi∑fi\bar x = \frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i}xˉ=∑fi​∑fi​xi​​

The second form uses frequencies fif_ifi​ (or class midpoints for grouped data).

Symbols: xix_ixi​: the data values, nnn: how many there are, xˉ\bar xxˉ (“xxx bar”): the mean.

The idea

Add all the values and divide by how many there are. With a frequency table, each value counts fif_ifi​ times, so multiply before adding and divide by the total frequency. The mean is the balance point of the dot plot.

Worked example

Data 4, 8, 6, 5, 7: the sum is 30 and there are 5 values, so xˉ=6\bar x = 6xˉ=6.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Median

n=2k+1: x(n+12)n = 2k + 1:\ x_{\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)}n=2k+1: x(2n+1​)​n=2k: x(n/2)+x(n/2+1)2n = 2k:\ \frac{x_{(n/2)} + x_{(n/2 + 1)}}{2}n=2k: 2x(n/2)​+x(n/2+1)​​

Middle value of the sorted data; not pulled by outliers.

Symbols: x(k)x_{(k)}x(k)​: the kkk-th value once the data are sorted from smallest to largest.

The idea

Sort the data first. With an odd number of values the median is the middle one; with an even number it is the average of the two middle ones. Unlike the mean, one extreme value hardly moves it.

Worked example

3, 9, 1, 7, 5 sorted is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: the median is 5. With 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 12 the two middle values are 7 and 8, so the median is 7.5.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Mode

Mo: max⁡fi\text{Mo}:\ \max f_iMo: maxfi​

The most frequent value (there can be several).

Symbols: Mo\text{Mo}Mo: the mode; fif_ifi​: the frequency of each value.

The idea

The mode is the most frequent value — the tallest bar. It is the only measure of centre that works for categories (favourite colour), and a data set can have two modes or more.

Worked example

2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, 5: the value 3 appears three times, more than any other, so Mo = 3.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Weighted mean

xˉw=∑wixi∑wi\bar x_w = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}xˉw​=∑wi​∑wi​xi​​

Symbols: wiw_iwi​: the weight (importance) of each value xix_ixi​.

The idea

When some values matter more (exam worth 60%, coursework 40%), multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the sum of the weights. With percentages the weights already add up to 1.

Worked example

A mark of 6 with weight 2 and a mark of 8 with weight 3: xˉw=12+245=7.2\bar x_w = \tfrac{12 + 24}{5} = 7.2xˉw​=512+24​=7.2 — closer to 8, because 8 weighs more.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Effect of a linear change

yi=axi+b ⇒ yˉ=axˉ+b,sy=∣a∣ sxy_i = a x_i + b \ \Rightarrow\ \bar y = a\bar x + b, \quad s_y = |a|\,s_xyi​=axi​+b ⇒ yˉ​=axˉ+b,sy​=∣a∣sx​

Symbols: sxs_xsx​, sys_ysy​: the standard deviations of the old and the new data.

The idea

Changing units (y=ax+by = ax + by=ax+b) changes the mean in the same way. The spread only feels the factor aaa: adding bbb slides every point, so the distances between them stay the same.

Worked example

Temperatures with mean 20 °C and s=4s = 4s=4 °C in Fahrenheit (y=1.8x+32y = 1.8x + 32y=1.8x+32): mean 1.8⋅20+32=681.8\cdot 20 + 32 = 681.8⋅20+32=68 °F, standard deviation 1.8⋅4=7.21.8\cdot 4 = 7.21.8⋅4=7.2 °F.

Measures of spread

Variance

s2=1n∑(xi−xˉ)2=1n∑xi2−xˉ2s^2 = \frac1n\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - \bar x^2s2=n1​∑(xi​−xˉ)2=n1​∑xi2​−xˉ2

Symbols: s2s^2s2: the variance, the mean of the squared distances to xˉ\bar xxˉ.

The idea

Measure how far each value is from the mean, square it (so signs do not cancel) and average. The second form — mean of the squares minus the square of the mean — avoids computing every deviation.

Worked example

2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: xˉ=5\bar x = 5xˉ=5, the squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 with sum 32, so s2=328=4s^2 = \tfrac{32}{8} = 4s2=832​=4.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Standard deviation

s=s2s = \sqrt{s^2}s=s2​

Sample (unbiased) version divides by n−1n - 1n−1 instead of nnn.

The idea

The variance is in squared units (cm²). Its square root, the standard deviation, is back in the units of the data: a typical distance of the values from the mean.

Worked example

With s2=4s^2 = 4s2=4 the standard deviation is s=2s = 2s=2: values are typically about 2 away from the mean 5.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Range

xmax⁡−xmin⁡x_{\max} - x_{\min}xmax​−xmin​

The idea

The simplest measure of spread: the largest value minus the smallest. It is quick, but it depends only on the two extremes, so one unusual value can make it huge.

Worked example

3, 6, 8, 9, 12, 17: range 17−3=1417 - 3 = 1417−3=14.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Coefficient of variation

CV=sxˉCV = \frac{s}{\bar x}CV=xˉs​

Compares spread between data sets with different means or units.

Symbols: sss: the standard deviation, xˉ\bar xxˉ: the mean.

The idea

A standard deviation of 5 is large for values around 10 but tiny for values around 1000. Dividing by the mean gives a relative spread without units, which lets you compare different data sets.

Worked example

Group A: xˉ=50\bar x = 50xˉ=50, s=5s = 5s=5, CV=0.10CV = 0.10CV=0.10. Group B: xˉ=10\bar x = 10xˉ=10, s=2s = 2s=2, CV=0.20CV = 0.20CV=0.20. B is relatively twice as spread out, though its sss is smaller.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Standard score

z=x−xˉsz = \frac{x - \bar x}{s}z=sx−xˉ​

Symbols: zzz: how many standard deviations xxx is above (or below) the mean.

The idea

zzz counts how many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. It lets you compare results from different tests: the higher zzz, the better the relative position.

Worked example

A mark of 75 where xˉ=60\bar x = 60xˉ=60 and s=10s = 10s=10: z=1.5z = 1.5z=1.5. A mark of 80 where xˉ=70\bar x = 70xˉ=70 and s=20s = 20s=20: z=0.5z = 0.5z=0.5. The 75 is the better result relatively.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

The normal distribution

Gauss curve

f(x)=1σ2π e−(x−μ)22σ2f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}f(x)=σ2π​1​e−2σ2(x−μ)2​

Bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean μ; σ sets its width. The total area under it is 1.

The idea

The bell is centred at μ\muμ and its inflection points are at μ±σ\mu \pm \sigmaμ±σ. A larger σ\sigmaσ gives a wider, lower bell — the area under it is always 1, so the peak height is 1σ2π\tfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}σ2π​1​.

Worked example

For N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1) the peak is 12π≈0.399\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.3992π​1​≈0.399; for σ=2\sigma = 2σ=2 it halves to about 0.199 and the bell is twice as wide.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

68–95–99.7 rule

P(∣X−μ∣<kσ)≈0.68, 0.95, 0.997(k=1,2,3)P(|X - \mu| < k\sigma) \approx 0.68,\ 0.95,\ 0.997 \quad (k = 1, 2, 3)P(∣X−μ∣<kσ)≈0.68, 0.95, 0.997(k=1,2,3)

Heights with μ=170\mu = 170μ=170 cm, σ=8\sigma = 8σ=8 cm: about 95%95\%95% lie between 154154154 and 186186186 cm.

Symbols: μ\muμ: the mean, σ\sigmaσ: the standard deviation.

The idea

For any normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within one σ\sigmaσ of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. Since the curve is symmetric, what is outside is shared equally by the two tails.

Worked example

Heights N(170,102)N(170, 10^2)N(170,102): 95% of people are between 170−20=150170 - 20 = 150170−20=150 and 190190190 cm; only about 2.5% are taller than 190.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Standardising

Z=X−μσ∼N(0,1)Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)Z=σX−μ​∼N(0,1)

X=182X = 182X=182 cm above: z=182−1708=1.5z = \frac{182 - 170}{8} = 1.5z=8182−170​=1.5.

The idea

Every normal variable becomes N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1) after subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. So one table of Φ\PhiΦ serves all normal distributions: convert the bound to zzz, then read the table.

Worked example

Scores N(500,1002)N(500, 100^2)N(500,1002): P(X<650)=Φ(1.5)=0.9332P(X < 650) = \Phi(1.5) = 0.9332P(X<650)=Φ(1.5)=0.9332.

Quartiles and box plots

Quartiles

Q1=P25,Q2=x~=P50,Q3=P75Q_1 = P_{25}, \quad Q_2 = \tilde x = P_{50}, \quad Q_3 = P_{75}Q1​=P25​,Q2​=x~=P50​,Q3​=P75​

Medians of the lower and upper halves of the sorted data.

Symbols: PkP_kPk​: the kkk-th percentile (k%k\%k% of the data lie below it); x~\tilde xx~: the median.

The idea

The median cuts the sorted data in two halves; the medians of the lower and upper halves are Q1Q_1Q1​ and Q3Q_3Q3​. Together they cut the data into four quarters with the same number of values — the box of a box plot holds the middle half.

Worked example

2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13: the median is 7.5; the lower half 2, 4, 5, 7 gives Q1=4.5Q_1 = 4.5Q1​=4.5; the upper half 8, 10, 12, 13 gives Q3=11Q_3 = 11Q3​=11.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Interquartile range

IQR=Q3−Q1IQR = Q_3 - Q_1IQR=Q3​−Q1​

Symbols: IQRIQRIQR: the spread of the middle half of the data.

The idea

IQRIQRIQR is the width of the box: the spread of the middle half of the data. Unlike the range, it ignores the extremes, so a single outlier does not change it.

Worked example

For the data above, IQR=11−4.5=6.5IQR = 11 - 4.5 = 6.5IQR=11−4.5=6.5: the middle half of the values spans 6.5 units.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Outliers

x<Q1−1.5 IQR∨x>Q3+1.5 IQRx < Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR \quad \lor \quad x > Q_3 + 1.5\,IQRx<Q1​−1.5IQR∨x>Q3​+1.5IQR

The idea

A value is flagged as an outlier when it lies more than 1.5 IQR1.5\,IQR1.5IQR beyond the box. These limits are the fences; the whiskers stop at the last value inside them and outliers are drawn as separate points.

Worked example

Q1=10Q_1 = 10Q1​=10, Q3=18Q_3 = 18Q3​=18: IQR=8IQR = 8IQR=8, fences 10−12=−210 - 12 = -210−12=−2 and 18+12=3018 + 12 = 3018+12=30. A value of 35 is an outlier; 26 is not.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Percentile position

Pk:  i=k100 nP_k:\ \ i = \frac{k}{100}\,nPk​:  i=100k​n

Round up; if it is a whole number, average that value and the next.

Symbols: iii: the position in the sorted list; nnn: the number of data.

The idea

PkP_kPk​ leaves k%k\%k% of the sorted data below it. Compute i=k100ni = \tfrac{k}{100}ni=100k​n: if it is not a whole number, round up and take that value; if it is whole, average the iii-th and (i+1)(i + 1)(i+1)-th values.

Worked example

n=30n = 30n=30 sorted values, P90P_{90}P90​: i=27i = 27i=27 is whole, so P90P_{90}P90​ is the average of the 27th and 28th values. For P15P_{15}P15​: i=4.5i = 4.5i=4.5, round up to the 5th value.

Grouped data

Relative frequency

hi=finh_i = \frac{f_i}{n}hi​=nfi​​∑hi=1\sum h_i = 1∑hi​=1

Symbols: fif_ifi​: the (absolute) frequency of class iii, nnn: the total, hih_ihi​: the relative frequency.

The idea

Divide each count by the total number of observations to get the proportion of data in each class. Relative frequencies always add up to 1 (or 100%), which makes data sets of different sizes comparable.

Worked example

Counts 3, 7, 10 out of n=20n = 20n=20: relative frequencies 0.15, 0.35, 0.50 — check: 0.15+0.35+0.50=10.15 + 0.35 + 0.50 = 10.15+0.35+0.50=1.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Cumulative frequency

Fi=f1+f2+⋯+fiF_i = f_1 + f_2 + \dots + f_iFi​=f1​+f2​+⋯+fi​

Symbols: FiF_iFi​: how many data are in class iii or below.

The idea

Add the counts as you go down the table: FiF_iFi​ is the number of values up to and including class iii. The last FFF equals nnn. Cumulative frequencies are what you need to locate the median and the quartiles.

Worked example

Counts 3, 7, 10 give cumulative frequencies 3, 10, 20. Half of n=20n = 20n=20 is 10, reached at the end of the second class.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Median of grouped data

x~=L+n2−Fi−1fi⋅c\tilde x = L + \frac{\frac n2 - F_{i-1}}{f_i}\cdot cx~=L+fi​2n​−Fi−1​​⋅c

LLL lower limit of the median class, ccc its width, Fi−1F_{i-1}Fi−1​ cumulative frequency before it.

The idea

Find the median class: the first class whose cumulative frequency reaches n2\tfrac n22n​. Inside it, assume the values are spread evenly and go forward the fraction of the class width that is still missing: n/2−Fi−1fi\tfrac{n/2 - F_{i-1}}{f_i}fi​n/2−Fi−1​​.

Worked example

Classes [0, 10), [10, 20), [20, 30) with counts 5, 8, 7 (n=20n = 20n=20). n2=10\tfrac n2 = 102n​=10 falls in [10, 20) (FFF goes 5 → 13): x~=10+10−58⋅10=16.25\tilde x = 10 + \tfrac{10 - 5}{8}\cdot 10 = 16.25x~=10+810−5​⋅10=16.25.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Histogram

H=hicH = \frac{h_i}{c}H=chi​​

With unequal widths, bar area (not height) shows the frequency; total area =1= 1=1.

Symbols: HHH: the height of the bar, ccc: the width of the class.

The idea

In a histogram the area of each bar, not its height, shows the frequency. With unequal class widths, divide the relative frequency by the width ccc to get the bar height (the frequency density); otherwise wide classes look too big.

Worked example

Class [0, 10) holds 20% of the data: height 0.210=0.02\tfrac{0.2}{10} = 0.02100.2​=0.02. Class [10, 30) holds 30%: height 0.320=0.015\tfrac{0.3}{20} = 0.015200.3​=0.015 — lower, although it holds more data, because it is twice as wide.

Correlation and regression

Covariance

sxy=1n∑(xi−xˉ)(yi−yˉ)=1n∑xiyi−xˉ yˉs_{xy} = \frac1n\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) = \frac1n\sum x_iy_i - \bar x\,\bar ysxy​=n1​∑(xi​−xˉ)(yi​−yˉ​)=n1​∑xi​yi​−xˉyˉ​

Symbols: sxys_{xy}sxy​: the covariance, positive when xxx and yyy tend to grow together.

The idea

For each point, multiply its distance from xˉ\bar xxˉ by its distance from yˉ\bar yyˉ​. Points up-right or down-left of the centre (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​) give positive products, the other two quadrants negative ones. The average sign tells the direction of the relationship.

Worked example

Points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5): xˉ=3\bar x = 3xˉ=3, yˉ=4\bar y = 4yˉ​=4, ∑xiyi=66\sum x_iy_i = 66∑xi​yi​=66, so sxy=665−12=1.2>0s_{xy} = \tfrac{66}{5} - 12 = 1.2 > 0sxy​=566​−12=1.2>0: yyy tends to grow with xxx.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Correlation coefficient

r=sxysx syr = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x\,s_y}r=sx​sy​sxy​​−1≤r≤1-1 \le r \le 1−1≤r≤1

∣r∣\lvert r\rvert∣r∣ near 111: strong linear relation; sign gives the direction; r≈0r \approx 0r≈0: no linear relation.

Symbols: sxs_xsx​, sys_ysy​: the standard deviations of xxx and yyy.

The idea

The covariance depends on the units; dividing by both standard deviations gives a pure number between −1 and 1. Near ±1 the points hug a line; near 0 there is no linear trend (though there might be a curved one).

Worked example

For the five points: sx2=11−9=2s_x^2 = 11 - 9 = 2sx2​=11−9=2, sy2=17.2−16=1.2s_y^2 = 17.2 - 16 = 1.2sy2​=17.2−16=1.2, so r=1.22⋅1.2≈0.77r = \tfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{2\cdot 1.2}} \approx 0.77r=2⋅1.2​1.2​≈0.77 — a fairly strong positive correlation.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Regression line of y on x

y−yˉ=sxysx2(x−xˉ)y - \bar y = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}(x - \bar x)y−yˉ​=sx2​sxy​​(x−xˉ)b^=sxysx2,a^=yˉ−b^ xˉ\hat b = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}, \quad \hat a = \bar y - \hat b\,\bar xb^=sx2​sxy​​,a^=yˉ​−b^xˉ

Always passes through (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​). Use it to predict yyy only inside the data range.

Symbols: b^\hat bb^: the slope, a^\hat aa^: the intercept; y^=a^+b^x\hat y = \hat a + \hat b xy^​=a^+b^x is the prediction.

The idea

The best line for predicting yyy from xxx passes through the centre (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​) with slope sxysx2\tfrac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}sx2​sxy​​. Use it to predict inside the range of the data; far outside, the prediction is unreliable.

Worked example

Same five points: slope 1.22=0.6\tfrac{1.2}{2} = 0.621.2​=0.6, so y−4=0.6(x−3)y - 4 = 0.6(x - 3)y−4=0.6(x−3), i.e. y=0.6x+2.2y = 0.6x + 2.2y=0.6x+2.2. Prediction at x=3.5x = 3.5x=3.5: y≈4.3y \approx 4.3y≈4.3.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Least squares form

b^=∑xiyi−nxˉyˉ∑xi2−nxˉ2\hat b = \frac{\sum x_iy_i - n\bar x\bar y}{\sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2}b^=∑xi2​−nxˉ2∑xi​yi​−nxˉyˉ​​

The idea

The regression line is the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances to the points as small as possible. Written with raw sums, its slope needs only ∑xi\sum x_i∑xi​, ∑yi\sum y_i∑yi​, ∑xiyi\sum x_iy_i∑xi​yi​ and ∑xi2\sum x_i^2∑xi2​ — the columns of a calculation table.

Worked example

Five points: b^=66−5⋅3⋅455−5⋅9=610=0.6\hat b = \tfrac{66 - 5\cdot 3\cdot 4}{55 - 5\cdot 9} = \tfrac{6}{10} = 0.6b^=55−5⋅966−5⋅3⋅4​=106​=0.6 — the same slope as before.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Coefficient of determination

R2=r2R^2 = r^2R2=r2

Share of the variation of y explained by the line.

Symbols: rrr: the correlation coefficient.

The idea

R2=r2R^2 = r^2R2=r2 is the share of the variation of yyy that the regression line explains. It is between 0 and 1 and loses the sign: r=−0.9r = -0.9r=−0.9 and r=0.9r = 0.9r=0.9 fit equally well.

Worked example

With r≈0.775r \approx 0.775r≈0.775 for our five points, R2=0.6R^2 = 0.6R2=0.6: the line explains 60% of the variation of yyy; the other 40% is scatter around it.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Line of x on y

x−xˉ=sxysy2(y−yˉ)x - \bar x = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_y^2}(y - \bar y)x−xˉ=sy2​sxy​​(y−yˉ​)

Both lines meet at (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​); the product of their slopes sxysx2⋅sxysy2=r2\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}\cdot\frac{s_{xy}}{s_y^2} = r^2sx2​sxy​​⋅sy2​sxy​​=r2.

The idea

To predict xxx from yyy, swap the roles: divide by sy2s_y^2sy2​ instead of sx2s_x^2sx2​. Both lines pass through (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x, \bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​); they coincide only when r=±1r = \pm 1r=±1, and the weaker the correlation, the wider the angle between them.

Worked example

Five points: sxy=1.2s_{xy} = 1.2sxy​=1.2, sy2=1.2s_y^2 = 1.2sy2​=1.2, so x−3=1⋅(y−4)x - 3 = 1\cdot(y - 4)x−3=1⋅(y−4), i.e. x=y−1x = y - 1x=y−1 (the steeper yellow line). The blue line y=0.6x+2.2y = 0.6x + 2.2y=0.6x+2.2 is the other regression line.

Contingency tables and χ²

Expected frequency

Eij=Ri CjnE_{ij} = \frac{R_i\,C_j}{n}Eij​=nRi​Cj​​

RiR_iRi​ row total, CjC_jCj​ column total, if the two variables were independent.

The idea

If the two variables were independent, the share of row iii would be the same in every column. So the count expected in a cell is (row total) × (column total) ÷ (grand total).

Worked example

In the table, cell (A,B)(A, B)(A,B): E=30⋅40100=12E = \tfrac{30\cdot 40}{100} = 12E=10030⋅40​=12, while 18 were observed — more than independence would predict.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Chi-squared statistic

χ2=∑(O−E)2E\chi^2 = \sum\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}χ2=∑E(O−E)2​

Large χ2\chi^2χ2 (beyond the table value for the chosen significance) suggests the variables are related.

Symbols: OOO: observed frequency in a cell, EEE: the expected one; the sum runs over all cells.

The idea

χ2\chi^2χ2 adds up, over all cells, the squared gap between observed and expected counts, scaled by the expected count. Zero means a perfect match; large values mean the data disagree with the hypothesis (compare with a table for the degrees of freedom).

Worked example

A coin tossed 40 times: 18 heads, 22 tails, against 20 and 20 expected. χ2=420+420=0.4\chi^2 = \tfrac{4}{20} + \tfrac{4}{20} = 0.4χ2=204​+204​=0.4 — very small, so no evidence that the coin is biased.

2 × 2 table

χ2=n(ad−bc)2(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)\chi^2 = \frac{n(ad - bc)^2}{(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)}χ2=(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)n(ad−bc)2​

Symbols: aaa, bbb (first row) and ccc, ddd (second row): the four counts; n=a+b+c+dn = a + b + c + dn=a+b+c+d.

The idea

For a 2 × 2 table you do not need the four expected counts: one formula with the cross products adadad and bcbcbc and the four totals gives χ2\chi^2χ2 directly. If ad=bcad = bcad=bc the rows are proportional and χ2=0\chi^2 = 0χ2=0.

Worked example

a=10a = 10a=10, b=20b = 20b=20, c=30c = 30c=30, d=40d = 40d=40, n=100n = 100n=100: ad−bc=−200ad - bc = -200ad−bc=−200, so χ2=100⋅4000030⋅70⋅40⋅60≈0.79\chi^2 = \tfrac{100\cdot 40000}{30\cdot 70\cdot 40\cdot 60} \approx 0.79χ2=30⋅70⋅40⋅60100⋅40000​≈0.79.
